The Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII) is the main US source of national
rates of **non-fatal** work injuries and illnesses. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)
estimates them each year from the OSHA logs of about 200,000 sampled employers. Read the module
[README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

The tables in `data/tidy/` are complete for the breakdowns they cover and are committed to the
repository.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/us-bls-soii/data/tidy")
read_tidy <- function(name) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name),
           col_types = cols(year = col_integer(), value = col_double(), .default = col_character())) |>
    mutate(across(any_of("display_level"), as.integer))
}

industry <- read_tidy("soii_industry.csv.gz")              # all recordable cases, 2014-2024
states <- read_tidy("soii_states.csv")
size <- read_tidy("soii_size.csv")
dafw_char <- read_tidy("soii_dafw_characteristics.csv")    # days-away cases, 2011-2020
dafw_detail <- read_tidy("soii_dafw_detail.csv.gz")
dafw_states <- read_tidy("soii_dafw_states.csv")

total_cases <- "Total recordable cases"
```

# Part 1. National trends

The **incidence rate** is the number of cases per 100 full-time equivalent workers:
cases / hours worked x 200,000.

```{r trends}
national <- industry |>
  filter(industry_code == "000000", case_type == total_cases,
         measure %in% c("injury_illness_rate_per_100", "injury_illness_cases_thousands"))

national |>
  filter(measure == "injury_illness_rate_per_100") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = ownership)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Total recordable injury and illness rate", x = NULL,
       y = "Cases per 100 full-time workers", colour = NULL)

national |>
  filter(measure == "injury_illness_cases_thousands", ownership == "Private industry") |>
  select(year, cases_thousands = value)
```

**Questions**

1. Describe the trend in the private industry rate. Why might rates have fallen?
2. State and local government workers have higher rates than private industry. Which
   government jobs might explain this?
3. What happened in 2020 to 2022? (Hint: how were COVID-19 cases recorded?)

# Part 2. Types of cases

```{r case-types}
industry |>
  filter(industry_code == "000000", ownership == "Private industry", year == max(year),
         measure == "injury_illness_rate_per_100", !str_starts(case_type, "RSE")) |>
  select(case_type, rate = value)

# Illness rates are per 10,000 workers
industry |>
  filter(industry_code == "000000", ownership == "Private industry",
         measure == "illness_rate_per_10000",
         str_detect(case_type, "^Total recordable cases of")) |>
  mutate(case_type = str_remove(case_type, "Total recordable cases of ")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = case_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Illness rates, private industry", x = NULL, y = "Cases per 10,000 workers", colour = NULL)
```

2. Which illness type is most common? Which illness spiked in 2020, and why?

   compared with injuries?

# Part 3. Which industries have the highest rates?

```{r industries}
latest <- max(industry$year)

industry |>
  filter(ownership == "Private industry", display_level == 3, year == latest,
         case_type == total_cases,
         measure %in% c("injury_illness_rate_per_100", "injury_illness_cases_thousands")) |>
  select(industry, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(desc(injury_illness_rate_per_100)) |>
  head(15)
```

**Questions**

1. Which industries have the highest rates? Which have the most cases? Why are the lists different?
2. Compare with the fatal injury rates in the CFOI module. Are the industries with the most
   non-fatal injuries the same as those with the most deaths? Why not?

# Part 4. States

Not every state takes part in the state-level survey.

```{r states, fig.height = 8}
states |>
  filter(ownership == "Private industry", case_type == total_cases,
         measure == "injury_illness_rate_per_100", year == max(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fct_reorder(state, value))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Total recordable injury and illness rate, private industry",
       x = "Cases per 100 full-time workers", y = NULL)
```


# Part 6. How precise are the estimates?

SOII is a **sample survey**, so every estimate has sampling error. BLS publishes the
**relative standard error (RSE)**: the standard error as a percentage of the estimate.

```{r rse}
rse <- industry |>
  filter(ownership == "Private industry", display_level == 3, year == latest,
         case_type %in% c(total_cases, paste("RSE of", total_cases)),
         measure == "injury_illness_rate_per_100") |>
  mutate(kind = if_else(str_starts(case_type, "RSE"), "rse_percent", "rate")) |>
  select(industry, kind, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = kind, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(se = rate * rse_percent / 100,
         lower_95 = rate - 1.96 * se,
         upper_95 = rate + 1.96 * se) |>
  arrange(desc(rse_percent))

head(rse, 10)
```

**Questions**

1. Which industries have the least precise estimates? Why?
2. Pick two industries whose rates look different. Do their 95% confidence intervals overlap?
3. The RSE describes sampling error only. Name a source of error it does **not** capture.

**Your answer:**



# Part 7. Cases with days away from work

For cases with **days away from work** (DAFW), BLS publishes details about the worker and the
case. These tables cover 2011 to 2020.

```{r dafw}
dafw_char |>
  filter(ownership == "Private industry", year == max(year),
         str_starts(characteristic, "Event")) |>
  select(characteristic, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(desc(cases))

dafw_char |>
  filter(ownership == "Private industry", measure == "median_days_away",
         str_starts(characteristic, "Age group")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = characteristic)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Median days away from work, by age", x = NULL, y = "Median days", colour = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which events cause the most days-away cases? Which cause the longest absences (median days)?
2. How does the median number of days away change with age? Why?
3. Find the musculoskeletal disorder (MSD) rows in `dafw_char`. What share of days-away cases are MSDs?

# Part 8. What SOII does not cover

SOII excludes the self-employed, workers on farms with 10 or fewer employees, private household
workers, volunteers, and federal government workers. It relies on what employers record on their
OSHA logs.

**Questions**

1. Compare the SOII estimate of private industry cases with the number of cases in the OSHA
   ITA case detail module. Why are they so different?

   estimated that SOII misses a large share of injuries. List three reasons employers' logs
   might be incomplete.
3. How would you design a study to estimate how many injuries SOII misses?
